parole.testo: From Middle Dutch aelmoesene, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic *alemōsinā, from Vulgar Latin *alemosyna, from Latin eleēmosyna, from Ancient Greek ἐλεημοσύνη (eleēmosúnē).

From Middle Dutch aker, eker, haker, from Old Dutch *aker, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], Latin aquarium. The loan from Latin is likely very early, as evidenced by the shifted consonants in Old High German ahhāri, ahari, agari. Doublet of aquarium.
From Middle Dutch averute, from Old Dutch *avarūta, from Proto-West Germanic *abrūtā, from Latin abrotonum, from Ancient Greek ἀβρότονον (abrótonon). Doublet of averoon.

parole.significato: butter, a spread made from churned milk
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch bōter, from Old Dutch *butera, from Proto-West Germanic *buterā, from Medieval Latin būtȳrum, from Ancient Greek βούτυρον (boúturon). Compare Limburgish bótter, West Flemish beuter, Zealandic beuter, Middle Low German botter, German Low German Botter, Plautdietsch Botta, Old Frisia

parole.significato: a container, a box, a tin
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch busse, from Old Dutch *bussa, from Proto-West Germanic *buhsā. Doublet of buks (“shotgun”), box, and pyxis.

From Middle Dutch dēken, from Old Dutch and Proto-West Germanic *dekan, from Latin decānus (“dean, chief of ten”). Compare Old High German tehhan(t) (Modern German Dechant). Doublet of decaan, a later borrowing.
From Middle Dutch duvel, from Old Dutch diuval, from Proto-West Germanic *diubul, from Latin diabolus, from Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos).

parole.significato: vinegar, especially dilute vinegar used as a drink
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch edic, from Old Dutch etig, from Proto-West Germanic *atek, metathesized variant of *aket, from Latin acētum. Cognate with Old Saxon edik, Middle Low German etik, West Frisian jittik, Old High German eȥȥih, German Essig, Old Norse edik. More distantly related to Old Saxon ekid, Old
From Middle Dutch eppe (“celery or similar plant”), from Old Dutch *eppi, from Proto-West Germanic *api, from Latin apium.

parole.significato: donkey, ass (Equus asinus or Equus asinus asinus)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ēsel, from Old Dutch esil, from Proto-West Germanic *asil, from Late Latin asellus.

From Middle Dutch gingebare, from Old Dutch *gingibero, from Proto-West Germanic *gingiberō, from Late Latin gingiber, from Latin zingiber, from Ancient Greek ζιγγίβερις (zingíberis), from Sauraseni Prakrit सिङ्गबेर (siṅgabera).
From Middle Dutch gokelare, from Old Dutch *gokalari, from Proto-West Germanic *kaukulārī, from Latin caucleārius. Equivalent to goochelen + -aar.

parole.significato: synonym of kaardenbol (“teasel, plant of genus Dipsacus”)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch caerde, from Old Dutch *carda, from Proto-West Germanic *kardā, ultimately from Latin carduus.
From Middle Dutch câse, from Old Dutch *kāsi, from late Proto-West Germanic *kāsī, borrowed from Latin cāseus.

parole.significato: domestic cat, pussy, Felis silvestris catus
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Dutch catte, from Old Dutch katta, *catta, from Proto-West Germanic *kattā, from Latin catta, feminine of cattus.

parole.significato: chain (a series of interconnected rings or links)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch kettinc, from the more common form ketene, from Old Dutch *ketinna, from ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *katinnjā, from Vulgar Latin *catenia, from Latin catēna.
From Middle Dutch cuekene, from Old Dutch *cukina, from Proto-West Germanic *kukinā, from Late Latin cocīna, from earlier coquīna.
From Middle Dutch kiste, from Old Dutch *kista, from Proto-West Germanic *kistu, from Latin cista, from Ancient Greek κίστη (kístē), from Proto-Indo-European *kisteh₂.

From early modern klokke, from Middle Dutch clocke, from Old Dutch *clocca, from Proto-West Germanic *klokkā, from Medieval Latin clocca, from Old Irish cloc, from Proto-Celtic *klokkos (“bell”), ultimately of onomatopoeic origin. In Early Modern Dutch, too, klokke still referred primarily to a bell
Inherited from Middle Dutch cort, from Old Dutch curt, from Proto-West Germanic *kurt, an early borrowing from Latin curtus.

parole.significato: underground cavity, vile and dark subterranean location
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch crocht, croft, from Old Dutch *krucht, *kruft (possibly attested in the placename Crochtem), from Proto-West Germanic *krufti, an early borrowing from Latin crypta, from Ancient Greek κρυπτή (kruptḗ). Cognate with Middle Low German kruft, German Gruft, Old English cruft. Doublet of
From Middle Dutch crône, from Old Dutch corōna, from Proto-West Germanic *korōnā, from Latin corōna. Doublet of kruin and corona.
From Middle Dutch crune, from Old Dutch *corūna, from Proto-West Germanic *korōnā, from Latin corōna. Doublet of kroon and corona.
From Old Dutch krucigon, from Proto-West Germanic *krūcigōn, from Latin cruciō.

From Middle Dutch quede, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], from Latin *quidōnea (see cotōneum, cydōnium), from Ancient Greek κυδώνιον (kudṓnion). The n seen in Latin and Greek was lost at some point after the Germanic borrowing from Latin, likely due to its re-interpretation
From Middle Dutch malve, maluwe, from Old Dutch *malwa, from Proto-West Germanic *malwā, from Latin malva. Doublet of mauve.

parole.significato: medlar; any tree of the genus Mespilus, now Crataegus sect. Mespilus
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Dutch mispele, mespele, from Old Dutch *mespila, from Proto-West Germanic *mespilā, from Late Latin mespila.

parole.significato: a mule, an equine crossbreed between a stallion (horse) and a she-ass (donkey)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch muul, from Old Dutch *mūl, from Proto-West Germanic *mūl, from Latin mūlus.
From Middle Dutch mente, minte, from late Proto-West Germanic *mintā (“mint”), from Latin menta. Doublet of mint.
From Middle Dutch offeren, from Old Dutch offeron, from Proto-West Germanic *offrōn, from Latin offerō. Doublet of offreren.
From Middle Dutch pert, pāert, from Old Dutch *pered, *perid, from Proto-West Germanic *parafred, from Late Latin paraverēdus. Compare German Pferd. Doublet of palefroot.

parole.significato: lease (in particular of land and immovable goods)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch pacht, Old Dutch *paht, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], from Latin pactum. Cognates include Old High German pfāht, Old Frisian pacht; the effects of the Germanic spirant law in these words and the effects of the High German consonant shift in the High German cognate in particular

parole.significato: pitch (sticky substance used as an adhesive and sealant)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Dutch pec, from Old Dutch pek, from Proto-West Germanic *pik, from Latin pīx. Cognate with German Pech (from which Dutch pech), English pitch.
From Middle Dutch poluwe, from Old Dutch *puluwī, from Proto-West Germanic *pulwī, from Latin pulvīnus.

parole.significato: pepper (Piper nigrum or the spice obtained from its berries)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch peper, from Old Dutch *pipar, *pepar, from Proto-West Germanic *pipar, from Latin piper, from Ancient Greek πέπερι (péperi), from an Indo-Aryan language.
From Middle Dutch perseke, from Old Dutch *persika, from Proto-West Germanic *persik, ultimately borrowed from Late Latin persicum, persica.
From Middle Dutch pijl, pile, from Old Dutch pīl, from Proto-West Germanic *pīl (“missile, arrow”), from Latin pīlum (“javelin, spear”).
From Middle Dutch pine, from Old Dutch *pīna, from Proto-West Germanic *pīnā.
From Middle Dutch pîpe, from Old Dutch *pīpa, from Proto-West Germanic *pīpā and Vulgar Latin *pipa, both from Latin pipō.

parole.significato: a plum tree, one of certain trees of the genus Prunus, especially Prunus domestica
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch prume, from Old Dutch *prūma. A variant of *plūma, from Proto-West Germanic *plūmā, from Latin prūnum, from Ancient Greek προῦμνον (proûmnon).
From Middle Dutch put, from Old Dutch *putti, from Proto-West Germanic *puti (“a well”), borrowed from Latin puteus.
From Middle Dutch rieme, from Old Dutch *riemo, from Proto-West Germanic *rēmō, borrowed from Latin rēmus.
From Middle Dutch schotele, from Old Dutch *skutala, from Proto-West Germanic *skutilu (“small bowl, dish”), from Latin scutella. Compare German Schüssel.
From Middle Dutch spīker, from Old Dutch *spīkāri, from Proto-West Germanic *spīkārī, from Late Latin spīcārium. Compare German Speicher, Old Saxon spīkari.

From Middle Dutch strâte, from Old Dutch strāta, from Proto-West Germanic *strātu (“street”), from Latin strāta, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sterh₃- (“to stretch out, extend, spread”). The geographical sense “strait” is a phono-semantic matching of Middle English streit, from Old French est
From Middle Dutch trachten, from Old Dutch *trahton, from Proto-West Germanic *trahtōn, from Latin tractō. Doublet of trakteren.

parole.significato: a flail, threshing tool (or by extension equivalent machinery)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vlegel, vleil, from Old Dutch *flegil, from Proto-West Germanic *flagil, likely from Latin flagellum (“whipping flail”).
From Middle Dutch vorke, from Old Dutch furka, from Proto-West Germanic *furkō, from Latin furca. Doublet of fork.
From Middle Dutch wan, wanne, Old Dutch *wanna, from Proto-West Germanic *wannu, from Latin vannus.
From Middle Dutch wannen, from Old Dutch *wannon, from Proto-West Germanic *wannōn, ultimately from Latin vannus (“winnowing basket”).

From Middle Dutch wijc, from Old Dutch *wīk, from Proto-West Germanic *wīk, from Latin vīcus (“hamlet, village, neighborhood”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyḱ- (“village, household”). Cognate with English wick, -wich, -wick, German Weich- in dated Weichbild (“municipal area”). Compare Gothic 𐍅𐌴𐌹𐌷𐍃 (

parole.significato: vetch, leguminous plant of the genus Vicia
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wicke, from Old Dutch *wikka, from Proto-West Germanic *wikkjā, from Latin vicia.
From Middle Dutch woensdach, from Old Dutch *wuodenesdag, from Proto-West Germanic *Wōdanas dag (“day of Woden”), calque of Latin dies Mercurii. Equivalent to Woen (“Wodan”) + -s- + dag (“day”).

From Middle Dutch saterdach, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic *Sāturnas dag, calque of Latin dies Saturni. Compare Low German Saterdag, West Frisian saterdei, English Saturday. Saturn or Saturnus is the sixth planet of the solar system, and it was the name of the Roman god of fertili
From Middle Dutch sēker, from Old Dutch *sikur, from Proto-West Germanic *sikur (“free, secure”), borrowed from Latin sēcūrus.

From Middle Dutch singroene, sindegroen, from Old Dutch *singrōni, from Proto-West Germanic *singrōnijā.
